title: ElasticMM: Efficient Multimodal LLM Serving with Elastic Multimodal Parallelism

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract (headline TTFT/throughput claims) vs. Introduction (contribution bullet), Section 4.2, and Section 6 Conclusion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract states 'reducing TTFT by up to 6.8× and achieving 5.1–7.2× higher throughput'. The Introduction contribution bullet states 'ElasticMM reduces TTFT by up to 4.2× and achieves a 3.2×–4.5× throughput improvement'. Section 4.2 reports TTFT reductions of 'up to 4.2× and 3.5×' (ShareGPT-4o) and 'up to 3.7× and 2.9×' (VisualWebInstruct), and throughput 'up to 4.5× and 3.2× higher throughput than vLLM'. The Conclusion states 'up to 4.2× reduction in TTFT and 3.2–4.5× higher throughput compared to vLLM'. The Abstract's 6.8× TTFT and 5.1–7.2× throughput figures appear nowhere in the main text and directly contradict the values repeated consistently in every other section.

The paper cites [21] as the source for the 'LLaMA-3.2 Vision' model: Section 2.1 says 'encoder-decoder architectures, including LLaMA-3.2 Vision [21]' and Section 4.1 says 'We select LLaMA3.2-Vision-11B [21]'. Reference [21] in the bibliography is 'Llama Guard 3 Vision: Safeguarding human-AI image understanding conversations' (arXiv:2411.10414, Chi et al.), a multimodal safety-guardrail classifier fine-tuned on Llama 3.2-Vision — not the Llama 3.2 Vision multimodal generation model whose architecture and results the paper evaluates. Verified via web search of arXiv:2411.10414, which describes a content-safety tool for prompt/response classification. No correct Llama 3.2 Vision reference appears in the bibliography.

The text states 'Recent work [22, 52] attempts to separate multimodal model inference stages, and Zhang et al. [61] proposed a similar two-tier separation in 2024 but lacked elastic scheduling.' However, the bibliography contains exactly 60 entries (indices [1]–[60]) and no reference [61] exists. 'Zhang et al. [61]' is therefore a fabricated/non-existent citation used to support a novelty claim about prior work. This is verified directly from the paper's own reference list.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1 (Modality-Aware Load Balancing), burst tolerance definition
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The prose defines burst tolerance as 'the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances', claiming this is 'as formalized in Equation 1'. But Equation 1 defines it as a ratio: 'bt(i) = (# Instances i can use for its peak load) / (# Instances i can use for its average load) = N_i^{peak} / N_i^{avg}'. A normalized difference and a ratio of peak-to-average instance counts are mathematically incompatible definitions of the same quantity, directly contradicting the equation the text claims to formalize. This undermines the stated load-balancing objective (maximize the minimum burst tolerance).

Proposition 1's proof claims 'these differences are typically on the order of ε ≈ 10^{-7} for fp16 operations' and later bounds probability variation with 'ε_max ≈ 10^{-7} for fp16 operations'. fp16 (IEEE half precision) has a 10-bit mantissa, giving a machine epsilon of 2^{-10} ≈ 9.8×10^{-4} (unit roundoff 2^{-11} ≈ 4.9×10^{-4}), not 10^{-7}. The value 10^{-7} is the machine epsilon of fp32 (2^{-23} ≈ 1.19×10^{-7}). The stated fp16 error bound is therefore off by roughly 3–4 orders of magnitude. The qualitative conclusion (differences are negligible) still plausibly holds, but the quantitative claim is wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix B.4, Lemma 3 (Dynamic Parallelism Invariance), Eq. (13)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Lemma 3's proof formalizes data parallelism as 'g_E^{DP_n}(i) = Gather({g_E^1(i_1), ..., g_E^n(i_n)})' where 'i_1,...,i_n represent partitions of input i'. This does not describe data parallelism: in DP the model is replicated across devices and the batch is sharded, with each device running the full model on its batch slice; a single image is not spatially partitioned across replicas. Independently encoding sub-partitions of one image with a ViT (which applies global self-attention over all patches) would not reproduce g_E(i), and 'synchronous all-reduce with fixed-order reduction' is not how DP outputs are concatenated. The proof's conclusion (parallelism does not change outputs) is true in practice, but the formalization in Eq. (13) is mathematically invalid.

summary: Uncertainty-mode verification of the ElasticMM paper (mode=uncertainty, strictness=lenient, uncertainty_threshold=0.30). The paper was segmented into 49 snippets; triage escalated 17 high-uncertainty snippets (uncertainty >= 0.30) to specialist verifiers (math, text, citation, statistics) plus a full-paper cross-section consistency check, and accepted 32 low-risk snippets without specialist review. 6 findings survived confidence filtering. (1) [0.92, cross-section] The Abstract reports headline gains of 'TTFT up to 6.8×' and '5.1–7.2× higher throughput' that appear nowhere in the main text and directly contradict the values repeated in the Introduction (4.2× / 3.2×–4.5×), Section 4.2 (up to 4.2× TTFT; 4.5×/3.2× throughput vs vLLM), and Conclusion (4.2× / 3.2–4.5×). (2) [0.88, citation] Reference [21], used for 'LLaMA-3.2 Vision' in Sections 2.1 and 4.1, is actually 'Llama Guard 3 Vision' (arXiv:2411.10414), a safety-guardrail model, not the Llama 3.2 Vision generation model evaluated — verified via web search. (3) [0.85, citation] The text cites 'Zhang et al. [61]' for a two-tier separation method, but the bibliography ends at [60]; reference [61] does not exist (fabricated citation). (4) [0.85, text] Section 3.1 defines burst tolerance as a normalized difference ('peak load minus idle capacity') while Equation 1 defines it as the ratio N_peak/N_avg — the prose contradicts the equation it claims to formalize. (5) [0.72, math] Appendix B.8 Proposition 1 states ε ≈ 10^{-7} for fp16 operations; fp16 machine epsilon is ~10^{-4} (10^{-7} is fp32's), off by 3–4 orders of magnitude. (6) [0.65, math] Appendix B.4 Lemma 3 Eq. (13) formalizes data parallelism by spatially partitioning a single input across devices, which is not how DP works and is invalid for ViT encoding. Additional lower-confidence concerns noted but not reported as findings (below confidence thresholds): promotional overclaim language in the Introduction ('completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks'), the Section 4.2 claim of 'universal applicability across all MLLM architectures' from only two tested models, the asymmetric testbed sentence ('ElasticMM was additionally tested with optimized CUDA kernels and custom memory allocators'), the Conclusion's 'guaranteeing SLO compliance under all workload conditions' and 'no significant limitations or risks', and the unexplained β vs. w penalty-factor change between Equations (2) and (3). The three high-confidence findings (abstract-vs-results mismatch, citation misattribution, fabricated reference) make the paper's headline numbers internally inconsistent and its references unreliable, warranting correction.
